beats.text: One processor. A keyboard, a disk, a screen, and a crowd of programs that all want it, right now.
Someone has to decide who gets what. That someone is the operating system.
It is a resource allocator: it shares out the CPU, the memory and the devices.
And it is a control program: it stops errors and improper use.
Its core is the kernel, the one program that runs the whole time the computer is on.
First puzzle. You press a key. How does the CPU find out?
One way is polling. The CPU keeps asking the keyboard: done yet? Done yet?
Almost every answer is no, and every question is wasted work.
The better way is an interrupt. The CPU gets on with real work. When the device finishes, its controller taps the CPU on the shoulder.
The CPU finishes the instruction it is on, and saves the program counter and the registers.
It looks up the interrupt vector to find the right handler, and runs that interrupt service routine.
Then it puts back what it saved, and carries on exactly where it stopped.
A trap is the software version: an interrupt caused by a program, for a request, or an error like division by zero.
Now the disk. It sends megabytes. One interrupt for every word would bury the CPU.
So it uses D M A, direct memory access. The device controller copies a whole block straight into memory, without the CPU.
And it interrupts once, when the block is done. One interrupt per block, not per word.
Last puzzle. What stops a program from simply taking over the machine?
The hardware does. One mode bit. One means user mode. Zero means kernel mode.
Privileged instructions, like talking to devices or setting the timer, only run in kernel mode. Try one in user mode, and the CPU refuses.
The only way in is a controlled door: a system call, a trap, or an interrupt. On the way out, the bit goes back to one.
And a program that just loops forever, never asking for anything?
Before handing over the CPU, the OS sets a hardware timer. When it runs out, it interrupts, and the OS is back in control.
For the exam.
The OS allocates resources and controls their use.
An interrupt replaces polling.
D M A: one interrupt per block.
Mode bit: one is user, zero is kernel.
The timer always gives control back.
